chapter_seo_title: Dao Guai Yi Xian Ch 495 – Big Boss: Zuowandao Finds Li Huowang at a Breakfast Stall
chapter_meta_description: The young emperor begs Li Huowang for help in a losing succession war. After dodging the trap, Li Huowang’s disguise is blown wide open by a friendly stall owner—his Zuowandao “Big Boss.”
og_title: Dao Guai Yi Xian Ch 495 – The Emperor Weeps, the Zuowandao Grins
og_description: Li Huowang turns down a doomed emperor, slips out of the city, and gets cornered by a cheerful street vendor who knows exactly who he is.
twitter_title: Ch 495: Li Huowang’s breakfast gets interrupted by a Zuowandao boss
twitter_description: The young emperor begs Li Huowang for help. He refuses. Then a fat stall owner asks for a “little favor.”

lore_anchors.definition: A sedan chair carried by eight bearers, the highest civilian honor in imperial China, reserved for top officials or direct imperial summons.
A traditional Chinese street breakfast: crispy fried youtiao folded around soft, sweet glutinous rice cake coated in black sesame and sugar.
A high-ranking title within the Zuowandao, corresponding to the Red Center tile in mahjong. Li Huowang previously held this rank.
A set of ancient rules binding the Supervisory Heavenly Office, including a prohibition against participating in court politics.

cultural_notes_faq.q: Why does the stall owner call Li Huowang “Big Boss”?
cultural_notes_faq.a: Because “Big Boss” (老大) is a Zuowandao code for a superior or handler. The plump vendor is a subordinate acknowledging Li Huowang’s former rank as a Red Center.

cultural_notes_faq.q: Is the young emperor going to die?
cultural_notes_faq.a: The narrative heavily implies he will be eliminated early in the succession war—he has no allies, no strategy, and is grasping at straws.

cultural_notes_faq.q: What does the die Li Huowang spits out mean?
cultural_notes_faq.a: The die is a Zuowandao calling card. Spitting it out signals that Li Huowang recognizes the vendor as a sect member, likely of equal or higher rank.
